The biopsy revealed diffuse cortical necrosis characterized by complete loss of viable cortical tissue, necrotic glomeruli, and fibrin thrombi occluding efferent arterioles and interlobular arteries (Figure 2). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel shows a B-mode ultrasound image consistent with a hypoechoic rim (reverse rim sign) in a patient with acute kidney failure and HELLP syndrome, supporting the diagnosis of acute cortical necrosis. B: Shows CEUS demonstrating loss of contrast enhancement in the right kidney, a sign of cortical necrosis, in a patient with acute kidney failure. C: Triplex sonography showing a normal resistance index of an interlobar artery in the context of renal pathology, supporting the overall clinical picture. D: Coronal CT scan showing a recess of contrast agent in both kidneys, which confirms the diagnosis of RCN in this patient.

panels.figure_caption: Example of RCN of the native kidney in a 28-year-old woman suffering from massive postpartum bleeding with acute kidney failure and HELLP syndrome. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: This panel is a B-mode US of a renal transplant showing a typical reverse rim sign associated with RCN. B: CeCT shows the hypoenhanced rim characteristic of acute cortical necrosis. C: CeMRI shows a hypoenhanced rim consistent with RCN. D: CEUS clearly identifies the reverse rim sign in the superficial cortex. E: CEUS using a linear probe confirms or refines the assessment for RCN. F: The parametric CEUS demonstrates arterial flow patterns consistent with the cortical rim sign. G: T2w MR confirms structural and perfusion abnormalities characteristic of RCN.
panels.attribution_text: Spiesecke et al. Multiparametric ultrasound findings in acute kidney failure due to rare renal cortical necrosis.. Scientific reports 2021. doi:10.1038/s41598-021-81690-x. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Comparison of modalities in the examination of a kidney transplant with suspected RCN. Upper row: Case showing partial RCN in a renal transplant in a 51-year-old man with end-stage renal failure due to shrunken native kidneys. (a) CEUS (0:59 min) and B-mode US of the renal transplant showing typical reverse rim sign with partial loss of enhancement in subcapsular cortex. (b,c) CeCT (b) and ceMRI (c) showing the hypoenhanced rim of the renal cortex in the transverse plane. Lower row: A case of RCN in a 54-year-old woman with renal transplant. (d) CEUS (1:13 min) using a convex multifrequency probe clearly identifies the reverse rim sign as a nonenhanced rim in the superficial cortex and lower pole (arrows). (e) Increased spatial resolution by use of a linear probe, which is important for second look if CEUS with convex probe shows inconclusive findings. (f) Parametric arrival time imaging of CEUS depicts arterial inflow in interlobar arteries and cortex within 4 s (red and green). Arrows indicate the so-called cortical rim sign with preserved blood supply by capsular arteries (arrows). (g) Coronal T2w MR image confirms the cortical structure defect and moreover shows cortical perfusion deficit at the upper pole of the renal transplant. RCN denotes renal cortical necrosis; CEUS, contrast-enhanced ultrasound; ceCT, contrast-enhanced computed tomography; ceMRI, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging.
in_text_mentions: Overall, nine patients underwent additional multiphase ceCT and two patients additional ceMRI, among them one patient who underwent ceCT and ceMRI (Fig. 3). In two patients, RCN detected by CEUS (one native kidney, one renal transplant) was not detected with ceCT. In these two cases, the maximum necrotic rim measured in CEUS was 2 mm and 3 mm. In the two patients who underwent both CEUS and ceMRI, the two modalities showed consistent findings.Figure 3Comparison of modalities in the examination of a kidney transplant with suspected RCN. of bilateral RCN19,20. These studies and our results consistently show that the reverse rim sign10 is adequately detected by CEUS. The reverse rim sign reflects loss of subcapsular enhancement (Fig. 3a–e, arrows) with preserved medullary enhancement and must be differentiated from the thin cortical rim sign (Fig. 3f, arrows) reflecting preserved supply by capsular arteries. Therefore, CEUS reliably reproduces the classical radiologic signs of RCN which are classically assessed in ceCT10.
